transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Kumar (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood), Elena Park (Saturnium CTO), Marcus Velez (Infra Lead), Priya Anand (Security), Jonas Li (SRE)

Summary: 30k-foot: walkthrough of air-gapped sealed image delivery, offline license activation, GPU driver signing, and KV cache warmup strategies. Agreed to run a driver+runtime smoke window and exchange signed manifests.

Topics: sealed images, artifact envelope, signed manifests, checksum verification, transport modality (sneaker-net vs airlock host), offline license tokens, device attestation, kernel module signing, GPU firmware versions, KV cache pre-warm, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization profile for 8-bit int8 friendly runtime.

Action items and next steps reviewed at the end.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, i'll kick off quick agenda — walk through the sealed image flow, offline license activation, and then ravi will deep dive into driver provisioning and runtime warmup, sound good?
[00:10] Elena Park: yep sounds good, we have about 40 minutes, want to focus on the parts that are most likely to break in an air-gapped environment — driver signing and the activation of the license token.
[00:18] Ravi Kumar: perfect. quick clarifying question — is Saturnium planning to have an airlock host that receives the bundle and then distributes to the cluster, or a physical medium (usb/hdd) \"sneaker-net\" transfer?
[00:25] Marcus Velez: for initial installs it will be sneaker-net, but eventual plan is an airlock appliance that we manage in an isolated DMZ.
[00:32] Maya Chen: ok good, that helps. we'll tailor runbook for both flows. note: our sealed-image is an OCI-like tar with a signed manifest, checksums, and an envelope that includes the offline license token blob.
[00:45] Jonas Li: couple things — how do we validate history of the manifest locally? do we need an HSM at the airlock or is a public key verify enough?
[00:52] Ravi Kumar: public-key sig verification is enough for the initial step; for stronger attestation you can have the airlock verify signature via an HSM or bring-your-own-KMS. The bundle includes a certificate chain and a deterministic manifest so the airlock can run a verify step before redistribution.
[01:08] Priya Anand: and the offline license token — is that a one-time activation or renews periodically? our security policy requires rotation every 90 days.
[01:16] Maya Chen: license tokens we provide are time-bound and support rotation. offline activation uses a signed nonce that gets consumed on first activation — we also provide a renewal flow where you generate a new token and exchange via the same sealed-image envelope.
[01:29] Elena Park: is the activation script interactive? we want automation to avoid manual key entry during installs.
[01:34] Ravi Kumar: we have a non-interactive mode: the install script accepts the sealed blob and an activation file; it validates signature, writes license to the node keystore and returns a machine-bound attestation record. We'll share a sample script. It does return human-friendly logs but no manual secret typing required.
[01:50] Liam O'Neill: slight note — in some on-prem installs customers want the license key only on the airlock appliance and not on nodes. we support that topology where the airlock holds the secret and serves a short-lived delegation token to nodes during install.
[02:05] Marcus Velez: ok that topology might be best for us, reduces blast radius. Next — GPU drivers. we run a mixed fleet of A100 and L40-like cards, what's the recommended approach for kernel module signing and firmware versions?
[02:18] Ravi Kumar: main points: (1) bundle includes prebuilt kernel modules signed with our key for validated kernels; (2) for customers that require OEM driver versions we provide a compatibility matrix — if you compile modules yourself you need to sign modules with your own key and enroll that key in the kernel keyring (we'll document the enroll step); (3) firmware diffs: we recommend matching on the firmware baseline in the manifest, we don't patch firmware during initial install in air-gapped mode unless explicitly requested.
[02:46] Jonas Li: will the runtime require specific kernel configs (e.g., hugepages, IOMMU flags) out of the box? We want to avoid surprises during our smoke window.
[02:53] Ravi Kumar: yes some sysctl/hyper params: hugepages, max_map_count tweak, and preemption settings — we'll include a preflight script. For performance the key ones are CPU governor set to performance and enabling kernel-page-table-isolation off for CUDA drivers if required (note: security tradeoff to discuss with Priya).
[03:13] Priya Anand: yep we need to chart that tradeoff. disabling some mitigations is sensitive. can we run a test workload under conservative settings first?
[03:20] Maya Chen: recommended approach: run conservative install first to validate stability, then in the smoke window toggle perf knobs and capture perf traces. we can help instrument the traces.
[03:28] Elena Park: on the manifest and checksums — what's your recommended hash and signing algorithm? sha256 vs sha512 etc.
[03:33] Ravi Kumar: sha256 is the default, signatures use RSA-4096 or ECDSA-p256 depending on your compliance needs. If you need FIPS-style we can output a FIPS bundle. The important bit is the chain and how the airlock verifies it.
[03:48] Marcus Velez: real-world gotcha we've seen: checksums changed during copy from host to usb because of a flaky controller — any recommended verification steps?
[03:57] Liam O'Neill: do a double-verify: after copy to the medium compute checksum, after copy to airlock compute checksum again and, if possible, sign the medium with a local ephemeral signing key. We'll include a small utility 'rfverify' in the runbook.
[04:12] Elena Park: let's talk runtime warmup — KV cache and batching. Our workloads have bursty short queries and also long-context generative jobs. How do we balance pre-warm vs memory pressure?
[04:23] Ravi Kumar: for bursty short queries prefix caching helps; we recommend a tiered KV warmup: (1) prefill the hot prefixes observed in the training eval set, (2) lazy load cold prefixes on first use with background prefetch, (3) maintain an LRU policy tuned to your sequence length distribution. We'll share suggested cache size percent relative to GPU memory.
[04:45] Jonas Li: are those prefills shipped as part of the sealed bundle? or generated after runtime spins up?
[04:50] Ravi Kumar: both options. we can ship a compact prefill artifact inside the sealed image for common prefixes, or run a one-time warmup job post-deploy using a benign prompt corpus. If you use the shipped prefill it's faster but increases bundle size.
[05:05] Marcus Velez: quantization — we want to use int8 to save memory, but concerned about latency variability. recommended quant profile?
[05:13] Ravi Kumar: quant profiles are workload dependent. int8 (sym/affine per-channel) generally gives 2-3x memory reduction with small accuracy loss. For latency stability we recommend quant+calibration with a small representative dataset and enabling per-layer fallback for layers that exceed error thresholds. We can provide calibration tooling.
[05:33] Maya Chen: to be explicit: in the bundle we'll include two model variants — quantized profile and fp16 profile — and runtime can prefer quant for capacity reasons with a fallback chain to fp16 if quality/latency thresholds are not met.
[05:48] Elena Park: you mentioned fallback — how does routing work without internet in air-gapped?
[05:53] Ravi Kumar: routing is local: we ship the policy in the config that the runtime consults. No external call needed. The policy lists fallbacks by local model artifact id.
[06:01] Jonas Li: about telemetry — we cannot phone home. what logs or metrics will we get in air-gapped?
[06:07] Maya Chen: we support a local observability bundle that writes tokenized metrics to a file or to your Prometheus endpoint inside the VPC. No outbound telemetry required. We also provide a manual export that can be scraped by the airlock for secure transfer.
[06:18] Priya Anand: does the local bundle include any PII or model data? we need to ensure nothing sensitive leaves the cluster during manual export.
[06:24] Ravi Kumar: by default export only system metrics and anonymized quality stats derived from prompts if you enable evals. You control which datasets are included in the export.
[06:33] Liam O'Neill: quick perf note — for initial runs use a warmup sequence length matching your 95th percentile; hot-starts reduce tail latency significantly. Also use batching thresholds tuned to latency SLOs.
[06:45] Marcus Velez: how big is the sealed bundle typically? for a model + prefill + drivers, estimate?
[06:49] Ravi Kumar: depends on model. a mid-sized open LLM quantized to int8 with prefill could be 45-60GB; with full fp16 variants and drivers could approach 120GB. We'll include a manifest that lists sizes for each artifact so you can plan media.
[07:05] Elena Park: license activation detail: if activation is done on airlock and a node never contacts airlock again later, will license become invalid?
[07:13] Maya Chen: activation yields a machine-bound key which doesn't require ongoing contact; rotation and renewals are separate flows. Airlock can provide delegation tokens if you want ephemeral leases.
[07:22] Jonas Li: what's the failure/retry pattern during installs — if checksum fails, does the script automatically retry or fail hard?
[07:27] Ravi Kumar: default behavior: fail hard and surface the mismatch. We have a flag to auto-retry with backoff, but for security we prefer explicit acknowledgement before automatic retries.
[07:36] Priya Anand: firmware — if there's a mismatch between GPU firmware and runtime expectations, do you block install?
[07:42] Ravi Kumar: we log a warning by default; for safety-critical installs we can enforce a hard block. That enforcement flag is in the manifest policy.
[07:51] Marcus Velez: ok good. Now a couple of edge cases: kernel panic during module load — what debugging artifacts should we collect in air-gapped environment?
[07:58] Ravi Kumar: capture dmesg, /var/log/kern.log, a kdump microdump if available, and the module's signed hash. We'll share a script to collect and package those artifacts for secure transfer off the air-gapped network.
[08:12] Maya Chen: switching gears — runtime tuning for latency: recommended batch size heuristics?
[08:18] Ravi Kumar: heuristics: set soft batch windows that prioritize latency SLOs, e.g., 10-20ms micro-window, with max_batch scaled to GPU memory. Use dynamic batching with a token-based cost estimator so the runtime avoids combining a long-context job with many short requests.
[08:33] Elena Park: if we have mixed workloads can we dedicate nodes?
[08:36] Ravi Kumar: yes you can pin model variants to node pools. Our scheduler supports label-based routing so you can keep high-throughput long-context on dedicated nodes.
[08:45] Jonas Li: regarding KV eviction policies — is LRU safe or do you recommend LFU for our workload?
[08:51] Ravi Kumar: for bursty patterns LRU is simple and often best; if you have stable repeated prefixes LFU helps. We can provide telemetry to recommend which to use.
[09:02] Marcus Velez: sample logs and the runbook — will you share as a single PDF artifact or a set of scripts?
[09:07] Maya Chen: we'll share a repo with bash/python scripts, a step-by-step PDF runbook, and the signed manifest templates.
[09:14] Elena Park: good. any known incompatibilities with some distros? we mostly run RHEL and Ubuntu LTS.
[09:19] Ravi Kumar: we test on RHEL 8/9 and Ubuntu 22.04; if you have RHEL 7 or custom kernels we may need to validate. We'll surface kernel ABI compat notes in the driver section.
[09:30] Priya Anand: security review items — will you provide your key rotation policy and compromise plan for offline license keys?
[09:36] Maya Chen: yes, we'll share our key lifecycle doc, rotation cadence, and a contact for incident handling.
[09:40] Marcus Velez: about the actual transfer medium — what's your recommendation for transport encryption on USB sticks? is AES-GCM encrypted tar enough?
[09:47] Liam O'Neill: AES-GCM or openssl enc with a key wrapped by the manifest's public key is fine. The important bit is integrity checks and signing as well. We'll include an encryption script in the runbook.
[09:58] Elena Park: one more thing — driver licenses: some OEM drivers require per-host licensing, will that conflict with Redwood's license model?
[10:05] Ravi Kumar: OEM driver licenses are separate; you must manage those with the GPU vendor. Our offline license covers the Redwood runtime and model serving; it doesn't replace OEM driver licensing.
[10:14] Jonas Li: quick note — on earlier projects we've hit stuck permissions when enrolling keys into kernel keyring, will your script handle that and provide escalation notes?
[10:20] Ravi Kumar: yes, script includes checks and prints steps to enroll keys and how to use mokutil if Secure Boot is enabled. We'll also provide signed module samples for mok enrollment.
[10:33] Maya Chen: ok we have about 30 minutes left; ravi can demo the driver install flow and then we'll walk through the sample manifest.
[10:40] Ravi Kumar: i'll share my screen (transcript note: screen share omitted) — first step: verify manifest signature: 
[10:44] [screen-share narration paraphrased] check: rfverify manifest.tar.gz.sig manifest.tar.gz 
[10:50] Ravi Kumar: second: decrypt sealed blob (if encrypted) using airlock-key, then extract drivers.tar.gz, runtime.tar.gz, model-quant.tar.gz. run preflight script which checks kernel headers, firmware versions, and available gpu memory.
[11:05] Elena Park: can the preflight fail safely without partial installs? we want atomicity.
[11:10] Ravi Kumar: preflight aborts before writing anything. actual install uses a staging area and only moves into place on success, so you get atomic-like behavior.
[11:22] Marcus Velez: sample timeouts for install? network-less installs can take long reading from media; any timeout tuning in scripts?
[11:29] Ravi Kumar: scripts have configurable timeouts; we default to disabled timeouts for media ops and recommend explicit size-based progress checks.
[11:38] Priya Anand: curious if you support signed kernel module rollback if an update breaks?
[11:44] Ravi Kumar: yes we keep a small number of previous signed modules in /opt/redwood/backup and our installer can roll back modules and firmware indices. The manifest lists rollback points.
[11:56] Maya Chen: we should recap next steps — Marcus you'll confirm test window, maya/ravi will send runbook + scripts, priya will enumerate compliance docs, and we'll schedule the smoke window. Anything else?
[12:11] Elena Park: also please include sample logs to collect and the packaging checklist for the transfer medium.
[12:17] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include that.
[12:20] Jonas Li: one more nit — are there any special SELinux contexts to set for runtime directories?
[12:25] Ravi Kumar: yes selinux preconfs are in the preflight script; we default to permissive if you choose to disable or we provide policy modules to set correct contexts.
[12:36] Priya Anand: ok sounds good. that'll be it from security side for now.
[12:40] Maya Chen: perfect thanks everyone. recap of action items we've captured and i'll send calendar invites for the smoke window.
[12:48] Elena Park: thanks all.
[12:50] [meeting end — transcript continues with a few post-call clarifications]
[13:05] Liam O'Neill: small clarification — the host airlock appliance can optionally run an HSM connector; if you use that we'll provide connector config.
[13:11] Marcus Velez: great, include that in the runbook.
[13:18] Maya Chen: will do. bye all.
